prompt: What is a test plan for, by this lesson?
hint: Before, not during.

choices.text: Listing every test case the team will run, step by step
choices.why: Cases have their own shape and change daily; the plan sits above them.

choices.text: Writing down the testing decisions before testing starts
choices.why: Right: made once, on purpose, where everybody can see them.

choices.text: Proving to an auditor that testing happened
choices.why: A record of testing is a report, made afterwards.

choices.text: Fixing the dates on which each tester works
choices.why: A schedule is one row of a plan, and it is written in dependencies first.

prompt: Which of these plan entries is the most useful?
hint: The lesson asks that every answer can be disagreed with.

choices.text: We will test thoroughly, to a high standard, across the whole product
choices.why: Nobody can object to it, so it decides nothing.

choices.text: Testing will follow industry best practice at every stage of the release
choices.why: Which practice? Nothing here can be checked or argued with.

choices.text: No Safari this release: 3% of visits, and no layout changes
choices.why: Right: a decision with its reason, which somebody can dispute in time.

choices.text: All important features will be covered
choices.why: Which ones are important is exactly the decision left unmade.

prompt: Match each question to the part of a plan that answers it.
hint: Seven questions, seven names.

prompt: A company tests twelve products and keeps one document saying which levels, tools and reports every project uses. What is that document?
hint: It sits above the plans.

choices.text: A master test plan
choices.why: A master plan belongs to one project and splits into level plans.

choices.text: A test strategy
choices.why: Right: the organisation's standing answer to "how", which each plan refers to.

choices.text: A level test plan for system testing
choices.why: That is one project's plan for one level.

choices.text: The definition of done
choices.why: That is one team's agreement about one story, not a company standard.

prompt: Why is the installed path the one the course recommends?
hint: Think about the tool a manual tester uses most.

choices.text: It is the only path that runs Python 3.10 or newer on every system
choices.why: All three paths have a recent Python.

choices.text: A virtual machine cannot run a web server that a browser can reach
choices.why: It can; the server is just harder to reach from your own browser.

choices.text: Your own browser reaches the application at 127.0.0.1 directly
choices.why: Right: testing happens in that browser, with nothing in between.

choices.text: It is free, while the other two paths both cost the student money
choices.why: A virtual machine costs nothing; only the online path has an allowance.

prompt: On Windows, with Python from python.org, which command starts the application?
hint: The course writes the Linux name.

choices.text: python3 boxoffice.py, as the transcripts write it
choices.why: On Windows that name can open the Microsoft Store instead.

choices.text: py boxoffice.py, or python boxoffice.py
choices.why: Right: both names reach the Python that python.org installed.

choices.text: curl boxoffice.py
choices.why: curl sends requests; it does not run programs.

choices.text: start boxoffice.py from File Explorer by double-click
choices.why: That opens and closes a window, and you lose the server's messages.

prompt: How do you reset boxoffice to the state every lesson assumes?
hint: Where does it keep its data?

choices.text: Delete the database file next to boxoffice.py
choices.why: There is none: everything lives in memory.

choices.text: Open /reset in the browser
choices.why: There is no such page.

choices.text: Stop it with Ctrl-C and start it again
choices.why: Right: nothing survives a restart.

choices.text: Copy the program again from the lesson
choices.why: The program is the same; the state is in the running process.

prompt: Why does boxoffice have an outbox page that the theatre's real system does not?
hint: Where would the e-mails go otherwise?

choices.text: So e-mails stop where a tester can read them, instead of going out
choices.why: Right: a test build should not mail real people.

choices.text: Because R3 asks for one
choices.why: R3 asks for the e-mail and its link, not for a page that lists them.

choices.text: So customers can read their e-mails in the browser when their inbox fails
choices.why: Customers read their own inboxes; the outbox is for testing.

choices.text: To keep a legal record of each message sent, as the theatre's lawyers asked
choices.why: It keeps nothing after a restart.

prompt: The page that answers `ok boxoffice 1.0` when the server is up is `/___`.
hint: Lesson 8 builds a smoke test on it.

prompt: curl answers `Couldn't connect to server`. What is the first thing to check?
hint: Nothing was listening.

choices.text: Whether curl is installed
choices.why: curl ran: it printed the error.

choices.text: The terminal where you started the server
choices.why: Right: it was closed, never started, or stopped with an error.

choices.text: Whether Python is older than 3.10
choices.why: An old Python fails when you start it, not when curl asks.

choices.text: Your network connection to the internet and its proxy settings
choices.why: 127.0.0.1 is this computer; the internet plays no part.

prompt: Where do you read the cause in a Python traceback?
hint: The rest is the path that led there.

choices.text: On the first line, after Traceback
choices.why: That line only announces what follows.

choices.text: In the middle, at the last line naming your own file
choices.why: That is where your code was, not what went wrong.

choices.text: On the last line, where the exception and its message are
choices.why: Right: OSError: [Errno 98] Address already in use, for example.

choices.text: In the server log, never on the screen
choices.why: The traceback is the error, printed where the program ran.

prompt: Match each message to what fixes it.
hint: One fix is a different directory.

pairs.right: Copy the file again with the button
Stop the other copy, or use BOXOFFICE_PORT

prompt: An IndentationError names line 57. One line lost two spaces; it is the line just above. Which line number holds the damage?
hint: The error often names the line after the damage.

prompt: What makes an item out of scope different from an item forgotten?
hint: Two things, written down.

choices.text: Out-of-scope items are tested later, in the release after this one
choices.why: Nothing says so; they may never be tested.

choices.text: Somebody wrote it down with a reason, and owns the decision
choices.why: Right: that lets the owners accept or refuse the omission.

choices.text: Out-of-scope items carry less risk, which is why they were left out
choices.why: Payment is out of scope here and carries plenty; it has another owner.

choices.text: Nothing: both are untested
choices.why: Both are untested, but only one was a decision.

prompt: Who knows most about a risk's likelihood, and who about its impact?
hint: They come from different people.

choices.text: The tester knows both, from what testing has already found
choices.why: The tester gathers both, from the people who know them.

choices.text: The business knows likelihood; the developers know impact
choices.why: The other way round.

choices.text: Developers know likelihood; the business knows impact
choices.why: Right: new or hurried code on one side, money and customers on the other.

choices.text: The customers know both, and a short survey finds them out
choices.why: Customers know some impact, and nothing of the code.

prompt: Two plans run out of time with a third of the cases unrun. One tested by risk, the other in the order the requirements are written. What differs?
hint: Which cases are in the third left over?

choices.text: Nothing: the same number of cases is left unrun
choices.why: The number is the same; which cases is not.

choices.text: The risk-based plan ran more cases in the time
choices.why: Ordering does not speed anything up.

choices.text: The requirements order is safer, because it follows the written specification
choices.why: Both are incomplete by a third.

choices.text: In the risk-based plan, what is left is what matters least
choices.why: Right: the price rule is not skipped for being written last.

prompt: Order boxoffice's risks as the lesson's grid ranks them, first to test first.
hint: High impact before low; within high impact, high likelihood first.
items: A refund reaches an order that should not have one
The shows table is hard to read on a phone
trap: Layout first would leave the price rule for the end, which is the plan this section warns about.

prompt: Which exit criterion can somebody who did no testing check?
hint: Checkable is the test.

choices.text: Testing is complete when quality is acceptable
choices.why: Acceptable to whom? Nothing to check.

choices.text: Cases for risks A to C passed, with no open critical or major defect
choices.why: Right: a list and a count anybody can look at.

choices.text: The testers feel confident in the release after two weeks of testing
choices.why: A feeling is real and cannot be checked by somebody else.

choices.text: The release date has arrived and the build has been deployed to staging
choices.why: That is running out of time, written as a criterion.

prompt: Why does the lesson write a test schedule in dependencies first and dates second?
hint: Testing waits for things.

choices.text: Dates are forbidden in a test plan by the standard that defines one
choices.why: They are not; they come second.

choices.text: Testers cannot estimate in days
choices.why: They can; the problem is what the dates hang on.

choices.text: A dependency survives a delay in development; a fixed date does not
choices.why: Right: "when booking is deployed" still means something after a slip.

choices.text: Dependencies make the testing go faster
choices.why: They make it start at the right moment, which is a different thing.

prompt: A new build arrives and the application does not start. What does the plan's suspension criterion say to do?
hint: A tester who keeps going writes one defect twenty times.

choices.text: Test whatever you can still reach and report each failure
choices.why: Every report would describe the same defect.

choices.text: Pause, and wait for a working build
choices.why: Right: report the one defect and wait.

choices.text: Move on to the exit criteria and finish the cycle
choices.why: Nothing was tested; nothing can be finished.

choices.text: Fix the build yourself and carry on testing
choices.why: The developer owns the fix; the tester reports it.

prompt: Which of these belong to boxoffice's test environment, as the plan describes it? Choose all that apply.
hint: Everything the application runs on or talks to.

choices.text: The version of the application, 1.0
choices.why: Yes: a different version is a different test.

choices.text: The four browsers named in R8
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: The outbox, standing in for the mail server
choices.why: Yes: what replaces a system is part of the environment.

choices.text: The defect reports written so far
choices.why: Those are deliverables of the testing, not something it runs on.

choices.text: The exit criteria
choices.why: They decide when testing ends; nothing runs on them.

prompt: The plan says "no Safari this release, 3% of visits". The manager says the theatre's main sponsor books on an iPhone. What has the plan achieved?
hint: When did the objection arrive?

choices.text: Nothing: it was wrong and the team must throw it away
choices.why: One row changes; the rest of the plan stands.

choices.text: It proved that the 3% figure from the analytics was false
choices.why: The 3% may be right; impact is not only a share of visits.

choices.text: It brought an objection in before the release
choices.why: Right: that is what a decision written down is for.

choices.text: It moved the Safari risk down to low likelihood on the grid
choices.why: The objection is about impact, and it raises it.
